Butler's "neither comfort nor performance" and "you come seeing among Danaans" are garbled; candidate gives sensible readings ("a good word or a good deed", "stand among the Danaans").
Source addresses Nestor as "Sir"; candidate says "Old friend", a small added familiarity. Acceptable.
Source "laughed out a loud applause"; candidate "broke into loud laughter" loses the applause nuance. Acceptable.
Source: "Adrestus and Amphius, whose breastplate was of linen" is ambiguous about whom it describes; candidate resolves it to Amphius alone ("Amphius wore a breastplate of linen").'

"peer of Jove in counsel" is rendered "the equal of Zeus in counsel" here but "peer of Zeus in counsel" at p47 (and "equal of the gods" at p26); "peer" is used for Ares at p46 and p49. Not in the STYLE-NOTE table; unify if desired.
Candidate adds the count "five captains"; Butler gives five names but no number. Harmless but technically an addition.

Source opens "Alexandria, also called Paris, challenges Menelaus"; candidate has "Paris challenges Menelaus". The double-name gloss is dropped, which is consistent with the STYLE-NOTE rule that Alexandrus is written Paris (recorded in ACCEPTANCE-RECORD.md). No fix needed.
Source Agamemnon addresses "Father Jove, that rulest in Ida"; candidate "you who rule from Ida". Harmless, and matches the wording used in p28. No fix needed.
Source: 'the sweat that I have sweated, to say nothing of my horses'. Candidate: 'worn out my horses besides' adds a result (worn out) the source does not state.
Source: "may we not now leave the Trojans and Achaeans to fight it out" is a proposal; candidate "why do we not leave..." reads as a rhetorical question; sense is close.
Source: "where the hip turns in the joint"; candidate "where the thigh turns in its socket" is a slight anatomical shift but sensible.

Source 'he had converse with the nymph' is a euphemism; candidate 'he slept with the nymph' is slightly more explicit but a sensible reading. Same softness shift in p13 ('would have had converse with me' -> 'wanted to lie with me').

Butler's "Sit down your own people" is garbled (and "at the hands of hands of Hector" is a typo). Candidate reads sensibly as "Go and sit down among your own people"; "Go and" is an interpretive addition.
Source 'may earth then swallow me'; candidate 'may the earth swallow me before then' shifts the timing slightly but is a sensible reading.
Source 'Minerva and Juno sat alone, apart from Jove'; candidate keeps 'apart from Zeus' but drops 'alone'.
Simile opener 'As when the stars shine clear' became 'Think of a night when the stars shine clear', a small added address to the reader; both halves of the simile survive.
Source 'honey-sweet corn' rendered 'honey-sweet grain' here, but 'corn' is kept elsewhere (p40, p41); minor inconsistency.
Butler's garbled 'sit upon knees' (no possessive); candidate resolves to 'sit on his knees', a sensible reading but ambiguous whose knees.
Source 'make havoc of the Achaeans'; candidate 'slaughter the Achaeans' is slightly sharper.
Butler’s 'exploit the Trojans' is evidently a garble for 'explore/spy on'; candidate’s 'scout the Trojans' is a sensible reading.
Butler’s 'Will to the ships and will exploit them' is a garble (likely 'spy upon'); candidate’s 'spy them out' is a sensible reading.

The Eilithuiae simile is restructured ("A woman in labor is sent sharp pangs by the Eilithuiae... The pangs that struck the son of Atreus were as sharp as those"). Both halves survive, but the order is slightly awkward for a general reader.
Source: "even so thick were the heads of them that fell by the hand of Hector"; candidate: "the heads of the men who fell... lay thick". Sense kept; "lay thick" is a small shift from "were thick".
Source: "Neleus was angered by what he had both said and done"; candidate resolves the pronoun to "what Augeas had said and done". Context (Augeas took the horses) supports it, so acceptable.
Source: Leonteus 'killed in combat' Antiphates; candidate adds 'close combat' (the sword is drawn, so harmless, but 'close' is not stated).
Butler's garbled "a redoubtable dispenser of death battle" (missing "in"); candidate reads sensibly as "a fearsome dealer of death in battle".

Source "sprang upon him like a vulture, drew the spear from his shoulder" leaves unclear whose shoulder (Ascalaphus's, from Deiphobus's throw); candidate keeps the same ambiguity ("sprang on him ... out of his shoulder"). Acceptable, but could name Ascalaphus.
Butler's text is garbled ('through the tops of when it is blowing its hardest', a word such as 'trees' or 'oaks' missing); candidate's 'through the treetops' is a sensible reading.
Source 'yet though these were fewer in number, they could not drive them back' leaves 'these' ambiguous; candidate resolves it as the Trojans being fewer. A sensible reading, but a choice.

Butler's source is garbled ('sprang upon Lampus was son of Laomedon'); candidate sensibly reads 'Dolops charged in. Lampus was a son of Laomedon'. Also source 'homed stag' typo at p21 is rendered 'horned' (correct).
Butler typo "cars" (ears) and "grip" (gully); candidate reads sensibly ("ears" implied by "rings in my ears", "gully").

Source “He knew that he was not to sack the city neither with nor without himself” has an ambiguous “he”; candidate resolves it to Patroclus (“Patroclus was not going to sack the city, with him or without him”). Plausible reading, but the pronoun is resolved to a named person.
Butler’s “I doubt that we shall not stay Hector” is garbled; candidate “I doubt that we can hold back Hector” takes a sensible reading.
Butler’s “at the loo of a band of young huntsmen” is a garbled/typo phrase; candidate “running at the head of a band of young huntsmen” is an interpretation not stated in the source.

Beacon simile: "in case they may come with their ships and help them" leaves the subject of "they" (the neighbors) unclear; Butler's "if so be that they may come with their ships and succour them" has the same looseness.
Source: "which the gods gave to Peleus when they laid you in the couch of a mortal man"; candidate: "on the day they laid you in the bed". "On the day" is a slight narrowing of "when".
Candidate opens the sailors' simile with 'Sailors at sea sometimes see', adding 'sometimes' and recasting Butler's 'As the light seen by sailors...even so'; both halves survive, so not a defect.
Candidate adds the rhetorical 'Think of it:' before 'many fewer Achaeans would have bitten the dust'; harmless filler not in the source.
Butler’s typo ‘You be low’ is read sensibly as ‘You lie low’ in the candidate; no change needed.
Source “took visible spear”; candidate resolves it to “took his spear” (Diomedes’s). Consistent with the poem but the source does not say whose spear.
Source: "then one whose parents are alive will drive him from the table"; candidate says "a boy whose parents are alive". Reasonable inference, not stated.
Source “Thus did they make their moan throughout the city”; candidate resolves to “the Trojans ... their city”. Supported by the end of Book 22, acceptable.
Source "Jove ... bids you come to him" / "so bid me" is softened to "calls you" / "call me"; also "lead at the end of an ox-horn" gains the word "line". Both are acceptable clarifications.
